title: Revised Recovery Plan for the Alaska-breeding Population of Steller’s Eider (Polysticta stelleri)

## Revised Recovery Plan for the Alaska-breeding Population of Steller’s Eider (Polysticta stelleri)

#### Revised December 2021 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Northern Alaska Fish and Wildlife Field Office Developed with the Steller’s Eider Recovery Team

Disclaimer 
The Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (16 U.S.C. 1531 et seq.), requires the 
development of recovery plans for listed species, unless such a plan would not promote the 
conservation of a particular species. Recovery plans delineate such reasonable actions as may be 
necessary, based upon the best scientific and commercial data available, for the conservation and 
survival of listed species. Plans are published by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, sometimes 
prepared with the assistance of recovery teams, contractors, State agencies and others. Recovery 
plans do not necessarily represent the views, official positions or approval of any individuals or 
agencies involved in the plan formulation, other than the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. They 
represent the official position of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service only after they have been 
signed by the Regional Director. Recovery plans are guidance and planning documents only; 
identification of an action to be implemented by any public or private party does not create a 
legal obligation beyond existing legal requirements. Nothing in this plan should be construed as 
a commitment or requirement that any Federal agency obligate or pay funds in any one fiscal 
year in excess of appropriations made by Congress for that fiscal year in contravention of the 
Anti-Deficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341, or any other law or regulation. Approved recovery plans 
are subject to modification as dictated by new information, changes in species status, and the 
completion of recovery actions. Please check for updates or revisions at the website below 
before using.

### 1. Introduction

1.1. Listing and review history 
The Steller’s eider (Polysticta stelleri), a small sea duck, occurs in three breeding areas – two in 
Arctic Russia and one in Alaska. Steller’s eiders that nest in western Russia and winter in the 
Barents and Baltic Seas comprise the Russia-Atlantic breeding population. Steller’s eiders that 
nest in eastern Russia and winter in the southern Bering Sea and northern Pacific Ocean are 
referred to as the Russia-Pacific breeding population. Steller’s eiders that nest in Alaska also 
winter in the southern Bering Sea and northern Pacific Ocean and are referred to as the Alaska 
breeding population; combined, Russia-Pacific and Alaska-breeding Steller’s eiders comprise the 
Pacific-wintering population (PWP). 
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service) was petitioned to list the global population of 
Steller's eiders as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 1991 (56 FR 19073). 
In 1992, the Service determined that listing the species as threatened was warranted but 
precluded due to other priority actions (57 FR 19852). During a subsequent status review in 
1994, the Service determined that listing the species range-wide was not warranted, but proposed 
the Alaska-breeding population be designated as a threatened Distinct Population Segment 
(DPS) due to the contraction of its breeding range in Alaska (59 FR 35896). The Final Rule for 
listing as threatened was published in 1997 (62 FR 31748). The Alaska-breeding population was 
designated as a DPS because it was considered both discrete and significant according to 
standards in Service policy (96 FR 4722). The population is discrete given its physical 
separation from both Russia nesting populations by hundreds of kilometers across the Bering and 
Chukchi Seas during the breeding season. In addition, the breeding areas are delimited by an 
international boundary that marks differences in conservation status as demonstrated by the 
higher abundance of the Russia-Pacific breeding population, and by differences in conservation 
laws and mechanisms for implementing conservation in the two countries. Because of 
uncertainty regarding the degree of movement between the two populations, genetic or biological 
factors were not included in the justification for discreteness. This is consistent with policy, as 
the Service’s DPS policy does not require absolute separation between two populations for the 
populations to be considered discrete. The Alaska-breeding population is significant because the 
loss of the population would represent a substantial reduction in the species’ breeding range 
worldwide (62 FR 31748). Critical habitat for Alaska-breeding Steller's eiders was designated in 
2001 (66 FR 8850). A recovery plan was published in 2002 (68 FR 20020). 
The Service completed a Species Status Assessment (SSA) in 2019 that synthesized the available 
information on the listed population of Steller’s eiders and assessed the population’s current and 
future viability. Here we summarize the results of the SSA which serve as the background for 
the development of this recovery plan. Service policy calls for the use of the conservation 
biology concepts of resiliency, representation, and redundancy (the 3Rs, Schaffer and Stein 
2000), which collectively describe the viability of a species, to assess species status and develop 
recovery plans (Smith et al. 2018:303). Resiliency refers to the ability of a population to 

withstand stochastic variation such as random variation in demographic rates. Commonly used 
metrics to measure resiliency include population abundance and growth rate. Redundancy is the 
ability of a species to withstand catastrophic events and can be measured by the number and 
distribution of resilient populations within the species’ ecological settings and historical range. 
Representation refers to the ability of the species to adapt to environmental conditions, which 
can be measured by such factors as behavioral and genetic diversity. 
The 3Rs concept is usually applied at the species level in SSAs, but because our primary interest 
in the Steller’s eider SSA was the likelihood that a population would persist over time (i.e., the 
Alaska-breeding population, a subset of the species) its application was more complicated. For 
example, a single population inherently has low redundancy, and it may be unreasonable to 
expect that additional populations will form, either naturally or with the aid of management 
actions. Because of the DPS designation, the Alaska-breeding population was largely considered 
isolated from the larger Russia-Pacific population in the SSA, while recognizing that some 
movement between the Alaska-breeding and Russia-Pacific breeding populations could occur. 
Based on this framing and the available biological data, the SSA characterized the Alaska 
breeding population as currently having low resiliency (low numbers present annually in Alaska, 
and highly variable vital rates), low redundancy (one extant subpopulation with a wide but sparse 
distribution in most of northern Alaska, with the exception of a higher concentration near 
Utqiaġvik), and moderate representation (adequate genetic diversity, varied diet and habitat use 
and wide distribution during non-breeding season [U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2019a:72– 
73]). Given the hypothetical but plausible future scenarios developed for the SSA, we predicted 
that resiliency (as measured by population abundance) of the Alaska-breeding population is 
likely to, at best, increase slightly or remain low. At worst, resiliency will decrease further due 
to the effects of climate change and continuing anthropogenic stressors. No increases in 
redundancy or representation under either plausible future scenario were predicted in the SSA 
(U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2019a:71). 
In 2019, a 5-year status review on the listed population concluded that the Alaska-breeding 
population of Steller’s eiders continues to meet the discreteness and significance standards for 
the same reasons as the original listing and should remain classified as threatened (U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Service 2019b:9). This plan revision was undertaken in response to the following two 
recommendations in the 5-year review. First, the demographic recovery criteria in the 2002 
recovery plan were based on estimates of extinction probability generated from a population 
viability analysis (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2002:9), but given uncertainty pertaining to the 
interconnectedness of the Alaska-breeding and Russia-Pacific breeding populations, our ability 
to estimate extinction probability is limited. Thus, the Service recommended that demographic 
recovery criteria be refined, or additional criteria be added, to improve our ability to measure 
progress towards recovery. 
Second, the Service recommended re-evaluating the criterion in the 2002 recovery plan that 
requires viable breeding subpopulations in both northern and western Alaska. Two 
subpopulations of Alaska-breeding Steller’s eiders were identified in the 2002 plan: the northern 
Alaska subpopulation, which may have historically nested from Wainwright, Alaska, east to 
nearly the Canadian border (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2002) and the western Alaska 
subpopulation, which may have historically nested on the Seward Peninsula, Yukon-Kuskokwim 

Delta (Y-K Delta), St. Lawrence Island, and possibly the Alaska Peninsula and Aleutian Islands (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2002). Since then, however, the criterion requiring a viable western Alaska subpopulation has come into question. When the Alaska-breeding population was listed in 1997, biologists were increasingly concerned about the status of nesting waterfowl in western Alaska, specifically on the Y-K Delta, one of North America’s most important waterfowl breeding areas. Spectacled eiders, a related species, had declined by 96 percent in the region (Stehn et al. 1993), and Steller’s eiders were hypothesized to have had followed a similar fate, albeit with little information about historical distribution and abundance in the region (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2019a). Since the early 1990s, the Y-K Delta spectacled eider population has increased, as have goose populations (Fischer et al. 2018), but Steller’s eiders remain rare and have not re-colonized the region in any measurable way. Additionally, despite a rigorous analysis of reintroduction of Steller’s eiders to the Y-K Delta, the Service found reintroduction to be an infeasible management tool due to high cost, low probability of success, and uncertainties related to habitat feasibility in a changing environment (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2017:7). At the same time, monitoring has demonstrated that a population of Alaska breeding Steller’s eiders has persisted in northern Alaska for several decades.
